Agreement No. CE 35/2023 (HY)
Development of the Loop: Eastern Connection Road -
Investigation, Design and Construction EIA Report
IMPACT OF CULTURAL HERITAGE
Introduction
This section presents the Cultural Heritage Impact Assessment (CHIA) findings of the
Project. The CHIA, which covers Built Heritage Impact Assessment (BHIA) and
Archaeological Impact Assessment (AIA), has been conducted in accordance with
the requirements given in Clause 3.5.11 and Appendix J of the EIA Study Brief (No.
ESB-375/2025).
The assessment area for CHIA is 300m from the Project Boundary
(60722948/A10/FIGURE 11.1 refers). Built heritage and archaeological heritage
within the 300m assessment area have been identified and the potential direct and
indirect impacts resulting from the construction and operation of the Project on the
identified built heritage and archaeological heritage have been assessed.
Appropriate mitigation measures have been proposed to alleviate the adverse
impacts as necessary.
Environmental Legislations, Standards and Guidelines
Legislation, standards and guidelines relevant to the CHIA include the following:
• Environmental Impact Assessment Ordinance (EIAO) (Cap. 499)1;
• Annexes 102 and 193 of Technical Memorandum on Environmental Impact
Assessment Process (EIAO-TM); and
• Antiquities and Monuments Ordinance (A&MO) (Cap. 53)4
.
Environmental Impact Assessment Ordinance (EIAO) (Cap. 499) and EIAO-TM
Annexes 10 and 19
The EIAO was implemented on 1st April 1998. It aims to avoid, minimise and control
the adverse impacts on the environment of designated projects, through the EIA
process and the Environmental Permit (EP) system.
According to Schedule 1 of the EIAO, Site of Cultural Heritage refers to “an antiquity
or monument, whether being a place, building, site or structure or a relic, as defined
in the Antiquities and Monuments Ordinance (Cap. 53) and any place, building, site,
or structure or a relic identified by the Antiquities and Monuments Office to be of
archaeological, historical or palaeontological significance.”5
Annexes 10 and 19 of EIAO-TM provide the criteria and guidelines for evaluating the
impacts to Sites of Cultural Heritage. It is stated in Annex 10 that all adverse impacts
to Sites of Cultural Heritage shall be kept to an absolute minimum and that the general
presumption of impact assessment shall be in favour of the protection and
conservation of all Sites of Cultural Heritage. Annex 19 provides the commonly

Antiquities and Monuments Ordinance (A&MO) (Cap. 53)
The Ordinance provides the statutory framework for preservation of objects of
historical, archaeological and paleontological interest and for matters ancillary thereto
or connected therewith. The Ordinance contains the statutory procedures for the
Declaration of Monuments. Under the Ordinance, a “monument” means a place,
building, site or structure which is declared to be a monument, historical building or
archaeological or paleontological site or structure under Section 3 of the Ordinance.
Excavations carried out on building works, demolition and interference of a proposed
monument or monument are prohibited except under permit under Section 6 of the
Ordinance.
Assessment Methodology
Following the requirement Clause 3.5.11 and Appendix J of the EIA Study Brief
(No. ESB-375/2025), the CHIA consists of a BHIA and an AIA. The assessment
methodology for BHIA and AIA are described below.
Built Heritage Impact Assessment (BHIA)
A desktop review was conducted to identify any built heritage within 300m
assessment area based on examination on the following resources:
• List of declared monuments and proposed monuments6;
• List of the graded historic buildings7
• List of new items for grading assessment8;
• List of Government historic sites Identified by Antiquities and Monuments
Office9;
Site visits were carried out in the assessment area on 29 April 2024 to evaluate the
current condition of built heritage identified during the desktop review, as well as any
items that might not be revealed by the desktop review.
The potential direct and indirect impacts on the built heritage during the construction
and operation phases of the Project have been assessed in the CHIA by following
the procedures and requirements of Annexes 10 and 19 of the EIAO-TM.
Mitigation measures are proposed in the CHIA for any affected built heritage to
minimise any adverse impacts when necessary.

Archaeological Impact Assessment (AIA)
A desktop review was conducted to identify any potential existence of archaeological
heritage based on examination on the following resources, when available: -
• List of Sites of Archaeological Interest10 identified by the AMO;
• Previous related EIA studies and archaeological reports;
• Related publications and monographs on relevant archaeological, historical and
geographical issues;
• Unpublished archival papers and records, and collection and libraries of tertiary
institutions; and
• Geological and historical maps, aerial photos and relevant visual archives.
The potential impacts that may affect the possible archaeological heritage during the
construction and operational phases of the Project have been assessed in the CHIA
by following the procedures and requirements of Annexes 10 and 19 of the EIAO-TM.
In case adverse impacts on archaeological heritage cannot be avoided, appropriate
mitigation measures would be designed and recommended in the CHIA to minimise
the impacts.
Project Background
Geographical and Geological Background
Physical Geography
The Project Boundary is located in Lok Ma Chau, New Territories, which is to the
south of Shenzhen River. It starts at the foot of Tai Shek Mo (大石磨; also known as
Crest Hill), running along the north of the hill of Lok Ma Chau, and ends at the Loop.
Currently, the terrestrial elevation within the Project Boundary is generally ranged
between +3.5mPD to +22.0mPD. Its gradient ranges from <1° to 10° in plains, and
gradually increasing to <30°
Past Landscape
Sea level rose approximately by 1m around 6,500 BP 11
. After a rise in sea level,
there was a drop in sea level approximately by 3m around 6,000 BP12 13
. The plain
(“QHH” and “Qam”) at the south of Shenzhen River was formed by sedimentation
less than 2,000 years ago14
.
According to the geology information, there were river valleys in the vicinity of the
Loop. The river valley was primarily shaped by Carboniferous Metamorphosed

Human Geography
Three villages are located in the vicinity of the Project Boundary, namely Ma Tso Lung
Shun Yee San Tsuen (馬草壟信義新村), Ma Tso Lung San Tsuen (馬草壟新村) and
Tse Koo Hang (鷓鴣坑). Ma Tso Lung Shun Yee San Tsuen (also known as Ma Tso
Lung Lutheran New Village) is located to the west foot of Tai Shek Mo. Meanwhile,
Ma Tso Lung San Tsuen is to the south of Ma Tso Lung Shun Yee San Tsuen. On
the other hand, Tse Koo Hang is located in a river valley to the south of the Project
Boundary. According to the aerial photo in 1924, part of Ma Tso Lung Shun Yee San
Tsuen and Tse Koo Hang were agricultural lands. In 196216
, Ma Tso Lung Shun Yee
San Tsuen was established. Ma Tso Lung San Tsuen (馬草壟新村) was constructed
between 197317 and 197418
. Tse Koo Hang was established between 1950s and
1970s according to the aerial photo19 and map20
.
Historical Background
Qin to Yuan Dynasties (221BC-AD1368)
Clues of human occupation within the south China can be found in historic textual
records such as Shiji (史記) and Hanshu (漢書), written in the first century BC and
first century AD respectively. These records describe that Yue ethnic groups (also
known as Hundreds of Yue (百越)) were scattered in southern China. The Yue ethnic
groups were comprised of different tribes bearing various surnames and can be
differentiated from the Han ethnic group who lived in central China in terms of physical
characteristics, language, and folklore.
The Yue people were gradually assimilated into the Han culture when southern China
became an administration territory of the central government since Qin dynasty (221-
206BC). During the Qin period, the Guangdong region was subordinated to Panyu
(番禺) County. In 208 BC, Southern Yue State (南越國) was established around the
Guangdong region by military officials, who were sent from the Qin Court to conquer
the Yue in the south. Following the collapse of Qin’s political power in the north, Han
dynasty (206BC-AD220)21 began. Southern Yue State was soon becoming a vassal
state of Han before integrated into the Han Empire.
Between Han and Eastern Jin dynasties (AD317-420), Hong Kong was subordinated
to Bolou (博羅) County22. From AD331 to AD756, Hong Kong was subordinated to

Ming to Qing Dynasties (AD1368-1912)
During the 15th century, the coastal areas of Dongguan County suffered from frequent
marauding bandit and pirate attacks. Xin’
an (新安) County was thus set up in
AD1573 to defend such attacks. According to Xin’ an Gazetteer (新安縣誌)24, the
modern region of Hong Kong fell within the Xin’an County.
In 1661, Coastal Evacuation Order was compelled by the Qing Court in order to stifle
the anti-Manchu troops in Taiwan. People living in coastal area were forced to move
50 li (里) (approximately 25 km) inland, including the New Territories inhabitants. The
Order was lifted in 1669. However, after the coastal evacuation, population dropped
severely. During the Shunzhi reign (1643-1661), the population of Xin’an County was
recorded as 6,851. The population dropped to 2,172 in 1664 during the enforcement
of the Order. After the Order was lifted, people were encouraged to move back to
Xin’an County during late 17th to early 18th centuries. In 1671, the population
increased to 3,972, 1,648 people were encouraged to move back during 1669-167125
.
After the First Opium War (1839-1842) between the Qing government and the British
Empire, the Qing government “…ceded … the Island of Hongkong, to be possessed
in perpetuity by … Great Britain” signed in 1842 under the Treaty of Peace, Friendship,
and Commerce Between Her Majesty The Queen of Great Britain and Ireland and
the Emperor of China (also known as the Treaty of Nanking (南京條約) ) 26
. The Qing
government lost the Second Opium War (1856-1860), which led to the ceding
Kowloon as a dependency of Hong Kong under the Convention of Peace Between
Her Majesty and The Emperor of China (also known as the Convention of Peking (北
京條約) ) in 186027

United Kingdom and China, Respecting an Extension of Hong Kong Territory (also
known as the Second Convention of Peking (第二北京條約) ) signed between the
British and the Qing government in 1898 allowed the British colony to “… enlarged
under lease … [for] ninety-nine years.”28

July 1997, it was announced that the new border between Hong Kong and Shenzhen
would be the centreline of Shenzhen River after the river training works29
. The
Shenzhen River Regulation Project was completed in 201730

These settlers in Ma Tso Lung initially settled on river plains near the farmlands,
which occasionally subjected them to flooding during rainy seasons. In the early
1960s, the formerly Swedish National Committee of Lutheran World Federation (瑞
典世界信義宗) (now known as Hong Kong Christian Service) recognised the poor
living conditions of the settlers. As a result, this organisation made donation and
constructed houses in Ma Tso Lung to improve the living standards of the settlers. In
1962, with the assistance of the North District Office and the Sheung Shui District
Rural Committee32, a new village was named Ma Tso Lung Shun Yee San Tsuen was
established in gratitude towards the Swedish National Committee of Lutheran World
Federation.
According to topographic maps, a cluster of buildings currently known as Ma Tso
Lung San Tsuen (馬草壟新村) was constructed between 197333 and 197434. It is
believed that these settlements were built by the settlers from Ma Tso Lung Shun Yee
San Tsuen and some immigrants from Dongguan35
. Meanwhile, Tse Koo Hang was
established between 1950s and 1970s according to the aerial photo36 and map37
.
In the late 20th century, an increase in the number of temporary structures scattered
within the river valley can be observed 38 . These structures overlooked the
surrounding farmlands, reflecting the ongoing agricultural activities in the region.
The geographical location of Lok Ma Chau is not only suitable for human settlements
but also border security. In 1951, the Frontier Closed Area was established under
the Frontier Closed Area Order to combat illegal migration and smuggling activities
across the border39. This action was taken in response to suspicious that some
border villages were smuggling equipment to mainland to assist Chinese armies
during the Korean War.40 As a result, the northern part of Ma Tso Lung, including
Shun Yee San Tsuen and Ma Tso Lung San Tsuen, was included within the closed
area.
Between 1949 and 1953, seven (7) observation posts were strategically constructed
along the territory border on hilltops to strengthen border defence 41
. These
observation posts later known as MacIntosh Forts, were named after Duncan
MacIntosh, the Commissioner of Police, who authorized the construction.

Archaeological Background
There is no Site of Archaeological Interest (SAI) identified within 300m assessment
area. Based on desktop review, several archaeological surveys were conducted by
others within Project Boundary and 300m assessment area. Details of the previous
archaeological surveys can be referred to 60722948/A10/FIGURE 11.3a.
Drainage Improvement in the Northern New Territories - Package B Archaeological
Survey Final Report43
In 2003, an archaeological survey was carried out as part of the Drainage
Improvement in the Northern New Territories - Package B Project. The project
involved the construction of drainage channels in Ma Tso Lung44
, which is partially
located within the Project Boundary of this Project. A total of fifteen (15) test pits and
one hundred and sixty-four (164) auger holes were excavated in Northern New
Territories. Among the test pits and auger holes abovementioned, two (2) test pits
and sixteen (16) auger holes were excavated in Ma Tso Lung area, of which two (2)
test pits and nine (9) auger holes are located within the Project Boundary of and 300m
assessment area of this Project.
Archaeological findings of Tang period kiln debris and pottery fragments dated to Han
and early Tang dynasty were found in the field survey, which is outside the 300m
assessment area of this Project (60722948/A10/FIGURE 11.3a refers). The findings
were “found as surface finds along the margin of two adjacent fish ponds on the
alluvial plain at Ma Tso Lung” 45
. That survey concluded that “[t]he broad-scale
disturbance of this area and conversion from paddy fields to fish ponds in the past 40
years has obscured much of the original landscape. Such disturbance may however
throw up the traces of settlements and activity during prehistory and the early historic
period…”46
A brief follow-up investigation is recommended to evaluate the nature and the extent
of the surface archaeological material found during this field work. With reference to
the report47, the evaluation should include:
• Field recording of the spatial distribution of surface finds at the margin of the
fish pond
• Preparation of cleaned 1m x 2m cross sections at the edge of the fish ponds
where pottery appears of highest concentration to establish (if any) horizontal
layers or depositional history
• The results of steps 1 and 2 will provide a basis for a program of 4-5 test pits in
the area of interpreted site focus

The report suggested that the fish ponds in the area only possess “low archaeological
potential”50
.
“Fragments of Tang period kiln debris and pottery dated to Han and early
Tang Dynasty (2nd to 7th Century AD) were found during field survey across an 80m
arc at the edge of two adjacent fish ponds - located about 500m northeast of the LMC
Loop area. The conversion from paddy fields to fish ponds in the past 40 years has
resulted in disturbance which – in this case – appears to have thrown up
archaeological remains from prehistory and the early historic period. Areas within the
LMC Loop occupied by dumped sediment and marshland have low archaeological
potential.” 51
Meanwhile, the low hill slopes at Ma Tso Lung area, including area in Shun Yee San
Tsuen and Ma Tso Lung San Tsuen, were considered to possess “moderate
archaeological potential” (60722948/A10/FIGURE 11.3b refers). The report
suggested that “these areas have moderate archaeological potential as sites of
prehistoric or early historic period occupation at the edge of the former shallow sea”52
.
Therefore, an archaeological survey was conducted under that project of the Planning
and Engineering Study on Development of Lok Ma Chau Loop in 2012, which
included these moderate archaeological potential areas. The survey including field
scanning, auger hole test and test pit excavation was conducted in the area along
Border Road, at Ma Tso Lung, Ma Tso Lung Road and Ho Sheung Heung Road. The
surveyed areas were located in hill slopes, margin of fish ponds and alluvium. The
then-proposed Eastern and Western Connection Roads were included in the survey
area.
Sixty-six (66) auger holes and twenty-one (21) test pits were excavated in this survey,
in which forty-two (42) auger holes and fifteen (15) test pits were located within the
Project Boundary or 300m assessment area of this Project. In particular, the survey
areas included 1) Border Road, 2) Ma Tso Lung and 3) Ma Tso Lung Road, which
fall into the Project Boundary of this Project. In total, eighteen (18) test pits and fifty-
two (52) auger holes were excavated in these survey areas. The survey findings did
not identify any sign of archaeological potential (Table 11.1 and
60722948/A10/FIGURE 11.3c refer).

• HB303 - MacIntosh Fort (Ma Tso Lung) (Grade 2 Historic Building)
(Appendix 11.1: LMC-01 MacIntosh Fort (Ma Tso Lung) &
60722948/A10/FIGURE 11.4 refer)
MacIntosh Fort (Ma Tso Lung) is an observation post serving the purpose of illegal
immigrant interception and border monitoring. It was built between 1949 and 195353
and ceased to operate in the 1980s54
.
The MacIntosh Fort is constructed of reinforce concrete and comprises a main
structure and two single-storey structures. It is surrounded by chain link fencing and
barbed wire. The structures are painted in green. One of the single-storey structure
is connected to the main structure from the south, and its purpose is unknown. The
remaining single-storey structure is located south of the main structures, and it served
as a bathroom.
The plan of the main structure is generally in the shape of an isosceles obtuse triangle
with rounded corners. Its apex is north facing while the two vertexes are south-east
and south-west facing. The main structure is also surrounded by projected eaves. A
two-storey circular (or octagonal) observation tower situated at the apex of the
triangular plan. The rest of the main structure is of one storey. Battlemented parapets
are installed above the roof and connected to the second storey of the observation
tower, so that an observation terrace is formed. Its design could be classified as
Modern Utilitarian55
.

iii. Survey along Ma Tso Lung Road
The tests either reached modern fill layers or regolith deposit.
That survey covered a large area in Ma Tso Lung and in vicinity of the Loop. And the
field data concluded that there is no sign of archaeological potential for these areas
(60722948/A10/FIGURE 11.3c refers).
Evaluation of Archaeological Potential
Although relatively flat areas were deemed suitable for past human settlement in both
prehistoric and historical periods as mentioned in the abovementioned reports64, the
survey results in 201265 has repudiated the presumption. Except the modern fill
layers found in some test pits, there was no cultural layer found between surface soil
and regolith layer. The absence of cultural layer, as well as other archaeological
findings, reflected that there is no sign of archaeological potential.
The Project Boundary and its 300m assessment area are located in the relative flat
areas near the hill foot. They are located in the same area sharing similar
environmental characteristics with the 2012 survey areas66 , which identified no
archaeological potential. Even though the 2012 archaeological survey did not
encompass the entire 300m assessment area and Project Boundary, the
environmental conditions of the unsurveyed portions are consistent with those of the
areas previously examined. On this basis, the conclusion of the 2012 survey, that
there is no indication of archaeological potential, can reasonably be extended to the
remaining areas of the current Project Boundary (60722948/A10/FIGURE 11.5
refers).
